title: Work, energy, power and conservation
blurb: Calculate work, kinetic and potential energy and power, apply conservation of energy, and explain efficiency, simple machines and the three lever classes.
question: A patient raises a 2.0 kg dumbbell 0.50 m in 1.0 s with a biceps curl. How much potential energy does it gain, what power does that take, and what class of lever is the forearm?

teach.body: Formally, work is done when a force moves an object along the direction of the force: W = Fd, in joules (1 J = 1 N·m). In general W = Fd cos θ, so only the part of the force along the motion counts. In plain English: no movement, no work; and a force at right angles to the motion does no work. Holding a heavy box still, or carrying a tray level at steady speed, does no work on it, however tiring it feels.

rows.label: Moving it
values: Lifting a box onto a shelf

rows.label: Direction
values: Pushing a cart along a hall
Holding a tray up while walking

rows.label: Against a wall
values: Sliding a box along the wall
Pushing a wall that stays put

teach.caption: Work needs displacement AND a force component along it. A vertical holding force does no work on a horizontal trip.

teach.body: Energy is the ability to do work, also in joules. Kinetic energy is energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Speed is squared, so doubling speed quadruples KE; doubling mass only doubles it. Gravitational potential energy is energy of position: PE = mgh, with h measured from a chosen level. The work-energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

items: Work: pushing a cart with 50 N for 4.0 m in the direction of motion. W = 50 × 4.0 = 200 J.
KE: a 2.0 kg ball at 3.0 m/s. KE = ½ × 2.0 × 9.0 = 9.0 J. At 6.0 m/s: 36 J, four times as much.
PE: a 5.0 kg box lifted 2.0 m (g = 9.8 m/s²). PE = 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 98 J.
Falling: dropped from 5.0 m (g = 10, no air). mgh = ½mv², so v² = 2gh = 100 and v = 10 m/s, whatever the mass.

teach.caption: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed in form. KE + PE stays constant when friction and air resistance are negligible.

teach.h: A 2.0 kg ball dropped from 5.0 m (g = 10 m/s²)
teach.caption: The total stays at 100 J the whole way down.

teach.body: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s); also P = Fv. A 100 W lamp uses 100 J each second. Efficiency = useful output ÷ input × 100%, below 100% in real machines. Simple machines (lever, pulley, ramp, wedge, screw, wheel and axle) reduce the force needed by making it act over a longer distance; they never reduce the work. Mechanical advantage = output force ÷ input force; for an ideal lever, effort arm ÷ load arm.

head: Class
In the middle
Examples
teach.caption: Most limbs are third-class levers: mechanical advantage below 1, but the hand or foot gains speed and range of motion.

teach.h: Scenario: Devon in the therapy gym
teach.body: Devon, a physical therapist assistant applicant, watches a patient curl a 2.0 kg dumbbell up 0.50 m in 1.0 s (g = 10 m/s²). PE gain = 2.0 × 10 × 0.50 = 10 J; power = 10 J ÷ 1.0 s = 10 W. The elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps pulls between the elbow and the hand, and the dumbbell is the load: a third-class lever. The muscle pulls harder than the dumbbell weighs, but the hand moves farther and faster.

teach.text: No displacement, or a force perpendicular to the motion, means no work. KE goes with v², not v. Dropped objects of different mass hit the ground at the same speed (the heavier one has more KE). Machines reduce force, not work, and no real machine is over 100% efficient. Power is a rate (J/s), not an amount. Convert grams to kilograms and centimeters to meters before using PE = mgh.

items: W = Fd along the motion (joules); a perpendicular force does no work.
KE = ½mv² (double v gives 4 × KE); PE = mgh.
Without friction KE + PE is constant; a drop from height h gives v² = 2gh.
P = W ÷ t in watts; efficiency = useful out ÷ in × 100%.
Machines trade force for distance. Lever classes: 1st fulcrum, 2nd load, 3rd effort in the middle.

summary: You can now decide when work is done and calculate work, kinetic energy, potential energy and power. You can also apply conservation of energy to falling objects, calculate efficiency and mechanical advantage and classify levers, including the third-class levers of the body.

A.q: In which case is work done on the object?
options: A guard holds a heavy box still
A student pushes on a wall that stays put
A waiter holds a tray up while walking level
A worker lifts a box onto a truck bed
A.why: Lifting moves the box upward in the direction of the lifting force, so work is done (W = Fd).

whyNot.0: Holding still means no displacement, so no work is done on the box.
whyNot.1: The wall does not move, so no work is done on it.
whyNot.2: The holding force is vertical and the motion horizontal, so that force does no work on the tray.

A.q: Which unit is used for both work and energy?
A.why: Work and energy are both measured in joules: 1 J = 1 N·m.

whyNot.0: The watt (J/s) is the unit of power, a rate.
whyNot.2: The newton is the unit of force.
whyNot.3: The pascal (N/m²) is the unit of pressure.

A.q: A 1,000 W microwave oven runs for 30 s. How much energy does it use?

whyNot.0: Divides power by time (1,000 ÷ 30) instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: Adds power and time, which have different units.

B.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 1,500 kg car moving at 20 m/s?
A 50 kg climber climbs 10 m up a rock wall. Using g = 10 m/s², how much gravitational potential energy does she gain?

whyNot.2: Adds a ½ that belongs to kinetic energy.

B.q: Which statement about an ideal ramp (inclined plane) is correct?
options: It reduces the work but not the force
It reduces both the force and the work
It reduces the force but not the work
It reduces both the distance and the force
B.why: A ramp lets a smaller force act over a longer distance. Ideally, work in = work out, so the work is the same.

whyNot.0: Reversed: the force falls while the work stays the same.
whyNot.1: No machine reduces the work needed.
whyNot.3: The distance increases; that is the trade for the smaller force.

C.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 1.8 m. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, what is its speed just before it lands?
C.why: mgh = ½mv², so v² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 1.8 = 36 and v = 6.0 m/s.

whyNot.0: 36 is v²; take the square root.
whyNot.2: Uses gh = 18 and skips both the 2 and the square root.
whyNot.3: Takes the square root of gh (18) and leaves out the 2.

C.q: A crane lifts a 200 kg beam 15 m in 10 s at steady speed. Using g = 10 m/s², what is its average power output?

whyNot.1: 30,000 J is the work; power divides it by the time.

C.q: A pulley system needs 250 N of effort to lift a 1,000 N load. The effort moves 8.0 m while the load rises 1.6 m. What is the system's efficiency?

whyNot.0: Inverts the ratio; no real machine exceeds 100%.
whyNot.1: Compares forces (250 ÷ 1,000) instead of work out over work in.
whyNot.2: 20% is the share of input energy wasted, not the efficiency.

reteach.title: Energy as a bank balance
reteach.question: If energy were money, what would work, power and a simple machine be?

blocks.body: Think of energy as money in an account that can never be printed or burned: it only moves. Work is a transfer from one account to another (your muscles to the box's PE). Power is how fast you transfer: the same $100 paid in one day or in ten is the same amount at different rates. A ramp is a payment plan: smaller payments (less force) over more installments (more distance), same total. Friction is a bank fee: some energy leaks away as heat.

blocks.text: A payment plan never lowers the total you pay, and a machine never lowers the work. It lowers the force.

explain.body: Multiply the force by the distance moved along it. Units: N × m = J.

test.q: A nurse pushes a hospital bed 12 m down a corridor with a steady 45 N force in the direction of motion. How much work does she do?

whyNot.2: Adds force and distance; work multiplies them.
whyNot.3: Halves the product; W = Fd has no ½.

explain.body: Multiply the speed by k and the kinetic energy is multiplied by k².

test.q: A cyclist's speed is halved. Her kinetic energy becomes:
test.why: KE is proportional to v²: (½)² = ¼.

whyNot.0: Treats KE as proportional to v; it goes with v².
whyNot.3: Cubes the factor; the exponent on v is 2.

explain.body: Without friction, mgh at the top equals ½mv² at the bottom, so v² = 2gh. Mass cancels.

test.q: A roller-coaster car starts from rest 45 m above the ground. Ignoring friction and using g = 10 m/s², what is its speed at ground level?

whyNot.0: Uses gh = 450 and skips the 2 and the square root.
whyNot.1: Takes the root of gh (about 21) and leaves out the 2.

explain.body: Ask what is in the middle: fulcrum (1st), load (2nd) or effort (3rd).

test.q: Which of these is a second-class lever, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort?
options: The forearm flexed by the biceps
test.why: In a wheelbarrow the wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the middle and you lift at the handles: second class.

whyNot.1: A seesaw has the fulcrum in the middle: first class.
whyNot.2: Tweezers have the effort in the middle: third class.
whyNot.3: The biceps pulls between the elbow and the hand: third class.
